source.title: Time-MoE: Billion-Scale Time Series Foundation Models with Mixture of Experts
source.authors: X. Shi; Shiyu Wang; Yuqi Nie; Dianqi Li; Zhou Ye; Qingsong Wen; Ming Jin

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. Some tables and figures are flattened or poorly rendered, but the relevant scaling claims are also described in text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in time-series foundation models, a different modality from the original language-model studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own model-size and training-data scaling results, plus downstream forecast performance. It does not fit or report power-law exponents, held-out pretraining cross-entropy, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or quantitative predictions from smaller runs. Comparisons of dense and sparse models and architectural ablations are not included as scaling-law results. References to prior scaling work are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: Trains three sizes of a time-series foundation model (50M/200M/1.1B activated) and saves data-scale checkpoints. It reports zero-shot and fine-tuned forecast MSE versus size and data, so it bears on whether scaling carries over to another modality (V5). It fits no power law and reports no exponents or extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say scaling laws hold for time series and that performance improves continuously with model size across all datasets, and with data. Correction: their own Tables 3 and 4 show non-monotone per-dataset results and near-flat averages, so 'across all datasets' is not supported by their numbers. They also conclude that MoE beats dense models at equal activated parameters or compute.
record.recipe_differences: This study scales sparse time-series forecasting models and evaluates forecast MSE/MAE; it does not reproduce language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law fits.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched activated parameters, sparse MoE models beat dense models in zero-shot MSE across data scales. MoE also cut training cost by 78% and inference cost by 39%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse MoE time-series models scale more compute-efficiently than dense models with equal activated parameters.

record.problems: The scaling results are qualitative in the text and no power-law fits, exponents, or extrapolation tests are reported. The data-scaling curves are presented in a figure without numerical values in the text. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-result rows were left out. Dense-versus-sparse comparisons and architecture/loss ablations were excluded because they do not report the scaling relationship itself.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; no power-law fit in N, D or C.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count. The top-k and ablation results are not shape-at-fixed-size tests.
Power-law form, exponents and fit quality untested (only three model sizes, no fit). Image/video, repeated data and transfer scaling untested.
No language-model downstream tasks; no relation of task performance to pretraining loss.
No analysis of fitting or setup choices on exponents.

missing.what: Per-dataset zero-shot avg MSE by model size, showing non-monotone scaling (ETTh1 ultra 0.412 worst; ETTh2 large 0.405 worst).
Per-dataset fine-tuned avg MSE by model size, showing non-monotone scaling on ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2 and Weather.
TaxiBJ short-term zero-shot MSE: large best (horizon 48: 0.414), ultra about equal to base (0.422 vs 0.423).
Data-scaling curves for each model size, sparse and dense.

record.verdict_notes: Three model sizes cannot establish a power law. The scaling claims are asserted from benchmark MSE rather than a fitted relationship. Model sizes also differ in depth (12 vs 36 layers), so size and shape are confounded. Zero-shot MSE on held-out datasets is treated as the closest analogue to held-out loss for V5.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures time-series forecast errors, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy or its dependence on parameters, tokens, and compute.
No power-law fits on small runs or predictions of much larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute sweep of parameter and token allocations or compute-optimal split is reported.
The study does not test effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests time-series forecasting as another modality, but does not fit a power law, report exponents, or test image/video modalities, repeated data, or transfer as a scaling-law form.
Reports downstream forecast performance across three model sizes, but does not predict larger-run task performance from smaller runs or relate task performance quantitatively to pretraining loss.
No sensitivity analysis of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations to fitting choices or setup is reported.

rows.baseline: Smaller T IME -M O E model sizes
rows.value: The authors report continuously enhanced performance as model size scales, across all datasets.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the three model sizes and six datasets; the paper does not give a fitted power-law curve or exponents for this result.
rows.check: Value overstates the trend. Table 3 avg MSE: ETTh1 0.400/0.394/0.412, ETTh2 0.366/0.405/0.371 (ultra not best on either). Overall average 0.336/0.336/0.322, flat from base to large. Only ETTm1, ETTm2 and Global Temp improve roughly monotonically. V6 link removed: V6 concerns language-model downstream tasks, and time-series scaling falls under V5.

rows.check: Table 4 avg MSE is non-monotone on several datasets: ETTh2 0.346/0.361/0.334; ETTm1 0.345/0.322/0.329; ETTm2 0.271/0.284/0.277 (base best); Weather 0.236/0.234/0.250 (ultra worst). Overall average 0.306/0.304/0.301 is a tiny gain. The value should give these numbers rather than 'continuous improvements'. V6 link removed.

rows.subject: T IME -M O E sparse models (aggregate across model sizes)
rows.size_stated: base: 113 M total parameters; large: 453 M; ultra: 2.4 billion
rows.operation_detail: Compared average forecasting error at different training-data volumes; checkpoints were saved every 20 billion time points.

conditions.value: different training-data sizes; checkpoints every 20 billion time points
average MSE for horizon-96 forecasting across six benchmarks

rows.value: The authors state that models trained on larger datasets consistently outperform those trained on smaller datasets, regardless of model size.
rows.locator: Section 4.4, Model and Data Scaling; Figure 3
rows.note: The text describes the trend; numerical values for the data-scale curves are not stated there.
rows.check: Rests only on the authors' text about Figure 3; curve values cannot be read, so the functional form (power law or not) cannot be checked. The direction (more data, lower MSE at every size) is observed as stated.

relationships.condition: Time-series MoE models, model size scaled base→large→ultra, zero-shot and one-epoch fine-tuned forecast MSE on six benchmarks
relationships.reason: Gains are uneven and non-monotone on several datasets: zero-shot average MSE is flat base→large (0.336/0.336/0.322), and fine-tuned gains are tiny (0.306→0.301). No power law is fitted (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Average zero-shot MSE was 0.336, 0.336, and 0.322 across increasing sizes, while fine-tuned MSE improved only from 0.306 to 0.301.

relationships.condition: Training-data volume scaled via checkpoints every 20B time points, horizon-96 zero-shot MSE
relationships.reason: The authors state that more data consistently lowers MSE at every size. The evidence is a figure with no readable values and no fitted functional form, so only the direction is shown (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Additional training data consistently reduced zero-shot MSE at every model size, without a fitted functional form.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
